articles.title: Warming and community context drive rapid plant evolution
articles.desc: Abiotic and biotic factors are important drivers of plant evolution, but how these factors interact to influence plant evolution in multispecies communities is still poorly understood. We performed experimental evolution exposing Brassica rapa plants to a combination of abiotic (ambient and hot temperatures) and biotic (visitation by bumblebees, butterflies or both) conditions. After six generations of selection, we grew plants at both temperatures and assessed floral divergence, temperature‐induced floral plasticity and complex patterns of non‐additive evolution. We found that the combined abiotic and biotic factors led to unique evolutionary trajectories: effects of warming on the evolution of plant traits and their plasticity were highly dependent on community context. Of all traits, the evolution of floral scent and its plasticity was most strongly affected by the combination of warming and biotic interactors, especially butterflies. We found abundant non‐additive effects that resulted from evolution in a multispecies community, and such effects were altered by warming. Complex interactive and non‐additive effects between abiotic and biotic factors will complicate predicting evolution in multispecies communities but provide crucial knowledge to understand rapid adaptation to current global change. articles.title: Dual mechanisms give rise to biphasic stomatal opening in onion
articles.desc: Stomata are controllable micropores on the leaf surface that regulate gas exchange and water loss. Pore aperture adjustment is a mechanical process whereby changes in guard cell turgor drive changes in cell shape, resulting in stomatal opening or closure. Previous computational models of kidney-shaped stomata primarily relied on guard cells elongating upon turgor increase, a process dependent on cell wall properties, such as anisotropy in stiffness, strain-stiffening, and polar fixing. Finite element method simulations using experimentally derived 3D meshes from confocal imaging of Allium cepa (onion) suggest an alternative mechanism for opening that is largely due to changes in guard cell cross-sectional shape. This mechanism does not rely on the assumptions for cell wall parameters required in previous models based on idealised geometries. We propose that mechanical responsiveness of guard cells to turgor changes is determined by a combination of two processes: one dependent on shape and the other on wall material properties. This suggests the parameters governing guard cell dynamics can be viewed abstractly as a two-dimensional (shape and material properties) 'morphospace', allowing multiple routes of shape adaptation to optimise gas exchange.

articles.title: Navigating shoot apical meristem plasticity for plant adaptation
articles.desc: Plants exhibit striking developmental plasticity, driven by stem cell populations within meristematic tissues such as the shoot apical meristem (SAM). While the genetic networks governing stem cell homeostasis are well-characterized, recent studies reveal that the SAM also functions as an active environmental sensor to modulate growth plasticity. This Tansley review synthesizes advances in how the SAM perceives and integrates key environmental signals - including light, temperature, oxygen, and humidity - to direct adaptive growth. We detail the molecular mechanisms, such as photoreceptor-mediated activation, thermal resilience pathways, hypoxia sensing, hydraulic dynamics, and mechanical signalling, that regulate stem cell activity. Furthermore, we explore how these environmental cues couple with developmental programs to fine-tune meristem function and organogenesis. By drawing parallels to the environmental regulation of root meristem development, we highlight conserved sensing and signalling modules within meristematic tissues that influence plant growth plasticity. Examining this interplay both in shoot and in root meristems, from evolutionary and applied perspectives, underscores how environmental responsiveness of stem cell niches regulates plant adaptation, informing strategies for engineering climate-resilient crops.

articles.title: Global transportation impacts on wildlife mortality and emerging pathways for mitigation
articles.desc: Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine transportation are fundamental to modern human life, but vehicle collisions with wildlife inadvertently kill hundreds of millions of animals across 2000 vertebrate and invertebrate species annually; however, a comprehensive framework to assess and mitigate these mortalities is missing. We identified and compared the most up-to-date information regarding the impacts of transportation on wildlife mortality to determine cross-cutting solutions to this challenging problem. For example, numerous strategies, such as under- or overpasses traversing roads and railways that increase wildlife-habitat connectivity, policies that enforce reduced speed in areas with active wildlife, and passive sensors that detect wildlife to alert nearby ships and vehicles and enable mandatory speed reductions, can reduce wildlife-vehicle collisions. We explored emerging technological advances that could help further reduce future wildlife-vehicle conflicts and provide a path forward for transportation systems. Specifically, we described how the combination of citizen science, artificial intelligence, targeted studies on wildlife demographic impacts, and cost-effective mitigation efforts will be powerful tools to inform needed future policies to decrease ship speed in areas with threatened whale species and reduce rates of wildlife mortality across ecosystems in a fast-moving world.

articles.title: Mitigating the human link in emerging reptile fungal pathogen transmission
articles.desc: Handling wild reptiles is common among amateur herpetology enthusiasts, professional researchers, social media influencers, and photographers. However, the potential for these interactions to spread diseases that threaten wild reptiles remains underappreciated. With the rise in such interactions due to today's socially connected landscape and the offering of an increased number of wildlife-focused ecotourism trips, the possibility of increased spread of human-vector-mediated reptile diseases is substantial. This spread is a concern, especially for novel and emerging potentially catastrophic fungal diseases such as ophidiomycosis (snake fungal disease). We summarized the current knowledge on the main fungal taxa of concern and associated disease, highlighting the threat of spreading reptile fungal diseases to new geographic regions and species via current practices, including direct- and indirect-handling and describing current mitigation strategies; developed key guidelines for practitioners and enthusiasts to reduce the risk of spread of disease; and identified areas of future research. This information will raise awareness and improve hygiene practices across the herpetology community to reduce the spread of disease and improve conservation.

articles.desc: Community perceptions of ecosystem services are shaped by individuals’ local contexts and their direct interactions with the environment. Examining these relationships enables a better understanding of how human perceptions of ecosystem services are associated with anthropogenic environmental change. In this study, we assessed the relationship between ecosystem service perceptions in riverside communities of semiarid reservoirs and sociodemographic variables, as well as the extent to which different land uses and land covers influence these perceptions. Interviews were conducted with residents living along the margins of the Sumé, Poções, and Cordeiro reservoirs (Paraíba River Basin) and the Sabugí, Passagem das Traíras, and Cruzeta reservoirs (Piranhas-Açu River Basin) in Northeast Brazil. Nevertheless, reservoirs surrounded by larger forested areas presented higher proportions of perceived regulation and maintenance services, whereas those with greater human occupation showed higher proportions of perceived provisioning services. The perception of provision services was negatively correlated with forest cover and positively correlated with human occupation. articles.title: The Too-Few Elephant Problem: Quantitative Analysis of Historical Elephant Tree-Toppling Rates Across Africa
articles.desc: Elephants were a major driver of tree stem mortality in Africa, but their impacts are now spatially constrained and they no longer topple trees across the continent. Thus, most African landscapes lack a key ecological agent that helped maintain diversity and functioning. Even ecologists living in Africa fail to anticipate the rampant destruction of trees that can occur when elephants live in and move through landscapes. If we can build in a consensus on the degree of above-ground tree turnover that is inherent in different contexts, it would inform restoration projects and ecological definitions of degradation. We collated empirical data on treefall in ecosystems with and without elephants and predicted past tree loss spatially. The metrics used (%trees or #trees ha −1 ) reveal assumptions about the processes controlling elephant damage. On average elephants knock down 5.4 [IQR 3.0–8.3] % of the trees in an ecosystem per annum. Mapping this into places that no longer contain elephants reveals the above-ground biomass turnover that would have been the norm for millennia before elephants were widely exterminated. On average, this is ~ 1/3 of woody biomass production but at a local scale it can often exceed production. There is an urgent need for better theory on elephant tree interactions, and restoration projects should embrace the rapid turnover dynamics these ecosystems evolved with.

articles.desc: Biological nitrogen (N) fixation is an important terrestrial ecosystem N input that occurs in both symbiotic and non-symbiotic associations with plants. The impact of non-native trees on galling and herbivory in New York City across space and time
articles.desc: Cities and suburbs frequently plant native and non-native trees as foundation species, with non-natives cultivated in these areas for centuries while remaining non-invasive. Although previous research has found that native trees often host more arthropods, studies have not simultaneously looked across space and time to determine the consistency of tree origin on urban arthropods. We combined varied methods across spatial and temporal scales in New York City to test if native tree leaves consistently have more insect and mite interactions than long-established non-native trees, predicting stronger effect sizes for specialists (galling arthropods) than generalists (herbivory). We examined (1) congeneric species pairs, controlled for growing conditions and stoichiometry in an arboretum, (2) diverse oaks at a botanical garden, (3) community science records across Brooklyn, and (4) herbarium specimens from 1883 through present across the city. Across spatiotemporal scales, we found consistent results. Specialist interactions were striking: contemporary native trees supported numerous galling species, while only one congeneric non-native species hosted any galls. For generalists, contemporary native trees had equivalent to slightly greater herbivory. Over the last century, herbarium records showed that herbivory increased on non-native trees to nearly the level of natives, whereas native trees increased in gall abundance while non-native trees remained rarely galled. articles.title: Less cooperative belowground plant mutualists negatively affect aboveground herbivore growth and survival
articles.desc: Resource mutualists like nitrogen (N)-fixing rhizobia can improve the quality of plants available to higher trophic levels, particularly primary consumers like insect herbivores. However, there is substantial variation in mutualist quality. How this variation in mutualist quality affects higher trophic levels, such as herbivores, is unclear, as high-quality resource mutualists could increase both leaf nutrient content, which should improve herbivore growth, but also plant chemical defenses, which are expected to negatively impact herbivores. We evaluated the effect of rhizobium strains of varying mutualist quality on the survival and development of a generalist insect herbivore, the beet armyworm (Spodoptera exigua), reared on alsike clover (Trifolium hybridum). We inoculated T. hybridum with cooperative ("high-quality") and less cooperative ("low-quality") rhizobia strains, measured plant growth, nutrients, and metabolites, and fed the leaves to S. exigua. We found that high-quality rhizobium strains significantly improved S. exigua survival, but also increased development time compared to low-quality strains. Furthermore, some developmental traits, such as pupal weight and adult wing area, increased in high-quality treatments. Inoculation with strains of varying quality impacted T. hybridum nutrition and phytochemistry, suggesting that both could mediate herbivore responses to mutualist quality. articles.title: Host tissue stoichiometry links nutrient availability to parasite abundance in a piscivorous fish
articles.desc: Understanding how ecosystem nutrient availability influences parasites is challenging, especially for trophically transmitted parasites in hosts occupying higher trophic levels. Host tissue nutrient stoichiometry may elucidate these effects by indicating nutrient availability within a host's environment and/or mediating these effects on parasites. We assessed these possibilities by manipulating nutrient availability in 11 experimental ponds stocked with piscivorous largemouth bass for 3 months and quantifying the role of a digestive tissue's stoichiometry in mediating the relationship between basal nutrient availability, the abundance of both fish and invertebrate consumers (including potential intermediate hosts), and the abundance of the trematode parasite, Crepidistomum spp., in this tissue. Fertilization increased the total phosphorus (P) and decreased the carbon (C):P and nitrogen (N):P ratios in the water column and fine particulate organic matter of ponds. While we did not detect effects of fertilization on intermediate trophic levels, N:P ratios in the bass digestive tissue were inversely related to both total water column P levels and the abundance of Crepidistomum spp. in these tissues. Overall, the nutrient ratios of a key tissue involved in predator digestion mirrored fertilization-induced shifts in basal nutrient availability and explained more variation in the abundance of a trophically transmitted parasite than any other variable we quantified. articles.title: Hyperabundance of a subordinate herbivorous gastropod causes localised overgrazing within kelp beds
articles.desc: Herbivory is a fundamental biological process that can determine the structure and functioning of ecosystems. On temperate reefs worldwide, herbivory by grazing macro-invertebrates can cause extensive overgrazing of kelp beds when grazers reach hyperabundance. Rising to local dominance, typically it is the grazing activity of a single species amongst others that is responsible for overgrazed 'barrens'. However, the potential for subordinate grazing species to impact kelp beds is less understood and often overlooked. Here we observe apparent 'barren' patches within kelp beds associated with local hyperabundance of a subordinate grazer, the turbinid periwinkle Lunella undulata, in eastern Tasmania. We demonstrate capacity for this periwinkle to overgraze by deploying a caging experiment on a 'peri-barren' patch, involving inclusion and exclusion treatments, plus cage and background control plots. Fleshy macroalgae proliferated in cages excluding periwinkles, reaching mean percentage cover of 47 ± 8% SE by end of the 117-day experiment, which was 5-fold, 6-fold, and 10-fold higher than in partially caged plots, open plots, and periwinkle inclusion cages, respectively. Indicating cascading effects of harvesting, legal-sized periwinkles were commercially harvested from the peri-barren during the study, leading to algal recovery across all treatments except for periwinkle inclusion cages where overgrazing persisted. articles.title: Bottom-up control of coral reef sponges: for better and for worse
articles.desc: Controversy over whether coral reef sponges are controlled bottom-up or top-down has distracted attention from more nuanced questions about what circumstances promote either bottom-up or top-down control, and how coral reef ecosystems are affected by what controls their sponges. Experiments now suggest that predators do not control coral reef sponges in their home habitat, shifting attention to effects of variations in sponge food supply. Comparing growth and survival of eleven of the most common and ubiquitous Caribbean coral reef sponge species on reefs in Belize and Panama differing in water column richness revealed faster sponge growth (by factors of 1.79-3.22 depending on the species) in the more picoplankton/nutrient-rich water at the Panama site. This could: a) benefit reefs by increasing positive effects of sponges, or b) harm reefs by sponges overgrowing corals. 'Sponges' is not a homogeneous category, so the balance between benefit and harm to reefs by increases in 'sponges' depends on both the species involved and environmental context. Predictions are complicated because sponge responses to increased nutrients/picoplankton are not monotonic: moderate increases boost sponge growth rates, but very dense blooms can devastate reef sponge populations. articles.desc: A global synthesis reveals that biodiversity is a major driver of ecosystem functioning and service delivery, and that biodiversity loss is likely to have widespread effects on people and ecosystems.

articles.title: Biodiversity safeguards ecosystem services and functions worldwide
articles.desc: An analysis of a global database of 423 studies and >200,000 data points outlines the strength and generality of biodiversity relationships with ecosystem functioning and services.

articles.title: Unifying bright spots research for people and nature
articles.desc: This Review presents a typology for how to identify and interpret bright spots, or positive deviance, in conservation and sustainability science, cases where unexpectedly positive outcomes occur despite local constraints.

articles.title: Interaction matrices as unifying tools for navigating ecological complexity
articles.desc: The interaction matrix is a widely used tool in community ecology. In this Review, the authors outline this approach and discuss how to tackle its challenges.

articles.title: Avian migration timing advances linked to season-dependent population benefits
articles.desc: Analysing a global database of migration timing for 549 bird species together with a full annual cycle theoretical model, the authors show that migration has advanced by >13 days since 1970 and that this has been beneficial in terms of abundance only in the pre-breeding migratory period.

articles.title: An ancient evolutionary origin for IL-1 cytokines
articles.desc: Protein-structure prediction identifies a family of IL-1 protein homologues in Eumetazoa, which are characterized for expression, localization and function in sea lamprey and purple sea urchin.

articles.title: Global patterns in plant-pollinator specialization
articles.desc: Pollination is a key ecological process sustaining biodiversity and food security, yet global patterns of plant–pollinator specialization remain unresolved. Using a global dataset of quantitative plant–pollinator networks (>3,400 networks, >110,000 interactions), we show that specialization is latitudinally structured, but not as a single directional pattern. We find no consistent monotonic increase or decrease in specialization towards the Equator. Instead, network-level and pollinator specialization peak at low northern latitudes near the tropical–subtropical boundary, whereas plant specialization is hemispherically asymmetric. Climate is most often the best-supported predictor of specialization compared with latitude, biodiversity and environmental productivity. Network-level specialization declines with increasing mean annual temperature, with strong group-specific differences. Precipitation exerts nonlinear effects: plant specialization peaks at intermediate precipitation but is lower at the wettest sites, whereas pollinator specialization is lower at intermediate precipitation, although often in interaction with temperature. Pollinator groups diverge strongly, especially in contrasting precipitation-related patterns between birds and insects. These findings show that global plant–pollinator specialization is structured by latitude and climate in complex and taxon-specific ways, with implications for uneven responses of pollination networks to future climatic change.

articles.title: N-glycosylation code diversifies paralogous chitinases to balance plant immunity and growth
articles.desc: This work reveals an N-glycosylation code that distinguishes two Arabidopsis chitinase paralogues, directing them to produce or degrade immunogenic chitin oligomers. This enables plants to gain chitin-triggered fungal resistance without a growth penalty.

articles.title: Maternal epigenetic regulation of embryonic patterning in plants
articles.desc: Post-fertilization remodelling of H3K27me3 in integuments regulates the timely activation of auxin transport genes, thereby facilitating maternal-to-embryo auxin transport and shaping embryonic patterning.

articles.title: SNI1 governs how temperature reshapes crossovers and genetic diversity
articles.desc: Cooler temperature alters the frequency and genomic sites of chromosomal DNA exchange during reproduction in Arabidopsis thaliana. This response depends on SNI1, a chromosome-architecture factor that acts as a temperature-sensitive brake on crossover formation.

articles.title: SNI1/NSE5 is a cold-sensitive brake on class II crossovers in Arabidopsis
articles.desc: Cold temperature alters meiotic recombination in Arabidopsis by weakening SNI1/NSE5, a chromosome architecture factor that normally limits class II crossovers and shapes where genetic exchange occurs.

articles.title: Long-term biomass growth unimpeded by short-term photosynthetic decoupling
articles.desc: Using long-term observations and global vegetation models, the authors show that the decoupling between photosynthesis and plant wood growth reported in recent studies neither implies sink limitation nor constrains long-term biomass growth.

articles.title: Engineering resilient forests
articles.desc: Climate change leads to changes in precipitation distribution and the frequency of extreme weather conditions. For temperate forests to survive this may require a targeted forest engineering approach.

articles.title: Impacts of needle-leaved forests landscape pattern and environmental factors on the spatial differentiation of pine wilt disease in China
articles.desc: Context. Following its emergence in China, pine wilt disease (PWD) has continuously expanded. Objectives: describing spatiotemporal dynamics of PWD in China 1982-2020. Methods: optimal parameters-based geographical detector (OPGD) model. Results: PWD expanded over four decades, landscape and environmental factors had high explanatory power. Conclusions: enhances ecological understanding of disease spread.

articles.title: Spatial distribution and environmental drivers of wild honey bee nesting patterns in the Eastern Cape Province, South Africa
articles.desc: Context: spatial clusters of animal nests driven by mating behaviors, social benefits, landscape heterogeneity. Objectives: characterize spatial distribution/environmental drivers of wild honey bee nesting in Eastern Cape, South Africa. Methods: surveyed 1km2 grid cells, beelining, Monte Carlo spatial randomness tests, GLMMs on 11 covariates. Results: 97 occupied nests in 16km2 across 5 sites; greater densities with rangeland, low land cover, high edge density low vegetation, southward downhill

articles.title: Landscape composition and photoperiod shape differences in space use and hunting behaviour between boreal and Alpine pygmy owl populations
articles.desc: Context: habitat specialists express population-level differences across landscapes/photoperiods. Objectives: space use, hunting habitat selection, diel activity in Eurasian Pygmy Owl boreal (Finland) vs subalpine (Italian Alps) populations. Methods: GPS-tagged 26 breeding males 2021-2024, AKDE home ranges, RSF GLMMs, cyclic GAMs. Results: forest specialists in both regions; boreal home ranges ~2x larger, daily movement ~1/3 greater. articles.title: Cross-scale influences of habitat and urbanisation on terrestrial vertebrates in coastal wetlands
articles.desc: Context: biodiversity in wetlands impacted by urbanisation; little known about terrestrial vertebrate use of mangroves/saltmarshes in Australia. Objectives: surveyed terrestrial vertebrates across estuarine seascapes with varying urbanisation. Methods: baited camera traps, 48h deployment, 7 estuaries, 115 sites (57 mangrove, 58 saltmarsh), SE Queensland. Emergent properties of urban landscapes shape urban eco-evolutionary dynamics
articles.desc: Context: urbanization creates novel selective pressures driving eco-evolutionary dynamics; role of urban spatial structure poorly understood. Objectives: test urban vs non-urban landscape heterogeneity differences and spatial property influence on eco-evolutionary feedbacks. Methods: 100 US metro areas, spatially explicit eco-evolutionary metacommunity model, plant-pollinator system. articles.title: How do green space cooling benefits align with population needs? A multi-dimensional assessment in a land-water mosaic city
articles.desc: Context: cooling efficiency of green spaces shows intra-urban heterogeneity, systematic assessments scarce. Objectives: Wuhan case study, framework for cooling benefits vs population needs. Methods: WRF-UCM model, UTCI, GWR analysis. Results: trees higher cooling efficiency than grass; cooling highest upwind SW regions. Conclusions: targeted landscape management strategies proposed.

articles.title: Identifying important areas for connectivity today and into the future: a spatial synthesis
articles.desc: Context: diverse connectivity maps pose challenges for spatial planning/climate change. Objectives: synthesize climate and non-climate connectivity studies for joint importance areas. Methods: reviewed 103 connectivity maps, western North America. Results: synthesis maps show modeling effort variation, agreement/divergence patterns, associations with elevation/human modification. Conclusions: helps planners draw insights from increasing connectivity analyses.

articles.title: Hydrogeological constraints amplify phenological responses of karst vegetation to climate variability relative to non-karst vegetation
articles.desc: Geological background remains an overlooked regulator of vegetation phenological responses to climate change. In particular, whether water- and soil-limited karst habitats amplify or attenuate vegetation phenological responses to climate variability remains poorly quantified. This study examined whether karst substrates amplify vegetation phenological responses to climate variability relative to non-karst regions and explored the underlying regulatory pathways. We integrated MODIS Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) time series (2001–2022), multi-source climate datasets, and carbonate rock distribution maps to assess vegetation phenological dynamics across karst and non-karst regions in subtropical Southwest China. Both regions exhibited an advanced start of the growing season (SOS), a delayed end of the growing season (EOS), and an extended length of the growing season (LOS). Although these fluctuations were generally synchronous between the two landforms, karst consistently showed larger anomaly magnitudes, particularly for earlier green-up and growing-season extension. Pixel-level RF–SHAP analysis further revealed greater proportions of pixels where negative climatic effects advanced SOS and positive climatic effects extended LOS in karst than in non-karst areas. This was further supported by PLS-PM evidence that the karst geological background indirectly shaped phenology via moisture limitation and drought stress. articles.title: Landscape configuration influences home range size and migratory movements of Carnabys cockatoos during the breeding season in fragmented mixed-use landscapes
articles.desc: Context: habitat loss/fragmentation major drivers of biodiversity decline. Objectives: investigate landscape configuration effects on home range size of breeding Carnaby's cockatoos (endangered). Methods: home range/seasonal movements at 5 breeding sites, landscape metrics, linear regression. Results: smaller home ranges at less fragmented sites; small patches providing functional connectivity in fragmented areas. Conclusions: importance of retaining habitat patches for animal movement.

articles.title: How do policy-oriented land use pathways reshape the urban-rural gradient structure of ecosystem service supply and demand? Evidence from Beijing, China
articles.desc: Context: supply-demand imbalance of ecosystem services core challenge under urbanization. Objectives: quantify how land-use pathways reshape ES supply-demand along urban-rural gradient, Beijing. Methods: 4 2035 scenarios (BAU/EDS/EPS/SDS), S-shaped functions. Results: carbon/water deficits narrowed, habitat quality deteriorated 15-fold; equilibrium point contracted 26.18km to 18.85-22.99km. Conclusions: ecology-oriented policies relocate rather than eliminate imbalance.

articles.title: Climate-mediated associations between landscape fragmentation and metropolitan forest resilience in subtropical China
articles.desc: Context: forest resilience under climate/fragmentation pressures insufficiently understood in metropolitan landscapes. Objectives: quantify/map forest resilience in Wuhan Metro Region 2004-2023. Methods: lag-1 temporal autocorrelation of NDVI, XGBoost/SHAP, SEM. Results: 60.54% of forests experienced resilience decline; patch shape complexity strongest association. Conclusions: critical role of fragmentation-climate interactions; need for adaptive forest management.

articles.title: Leveraging time-series remote sensing to predict post-fire invasive annual grass response in western US rangelands
articles.desc: Context: relationship between exotic annual grass (EAG) expansion, drought, fire frequency complex but critical. Objectives: quantify wildfire impacts on EAGs, drivers of variability, role of drought. Methods: 1985-2024 and 2016-2024 EAG cover datasets. Results: fire impacts on EAG often delayed; low pre-fire cover sites show greatest post-fire increase potential. Conclusions: critical insight for land managers on fire-EAG risk.

articles.title: Intermediate habitat fragmentation reduces gastropod movement in experimental intertidal landscapes: implications for fragmentation-diversity relationships
articles.desc: Context: experimental tests isolating fragmentation from habitat area rare; prior work found unimodal species-fragmentation relationship. Objectives: test whether intermediate fragmentation generates strongest dispersal limitation via reduced gastropod movement. Methods: experimental intertidal landscapes, tile cover x spatial configuration, drone surveys, mark-recapture. Results: movement distances lowest in several-small-patches configuration at 14% cover. Conclusion: supports dispersal limita

articles.title: Context-dependent effects of land-sparing and land-sharing strategies on urban bird diversity
articles.desc: Context: land sparing (LSP) vs land sharing (LSH) relative benefits for urban bird diversity poorly understood across gradients. Objectives: compare LSP/LSH effects on bird diversity by green-cover, residency, season, Nanjing China. Methods: 116,387 citizen-science records 2022-2024, diversity indices, GAMs. Results: LSP associated with higher diversity for residents below 50% green cover; LSH favors migratory birds above 50% cover. Conclusions: outcomes cannot be generalized without accounting

articles.title: Assessing the impact of sea level rise on landscape connectivity of forests and wetlands in coastal Southeast USA
articles.desc: Context: sea level rise disrupts terrestrial linkages, intensifies erosion, fragments habitat. Objectives: analytical approach for SLR impacts on omni-directional landscape connectivity, Chatham/St Johns counties. Methods: omnidirectional circuit theory, SLR scenarios through 2100. Results: Chatham faces more severe decline (17-50%) vs St Johns (14-19%); core area size correlates with vulnerability. Conclusions: direct applications for coastal resilience planning.

articles.title: Nonlinear associations between comprehensive ecosystem services and four compound climate extremes: a comparative analysis across China from 2000 to 2020
articles.desc: Context: compound climate extremes pose growing risks to ecosystem services via complex spatial associations. Objectives: characterize spatiotemporal dynamics of climate extremes/ES/CES 2000-2020, compare nonlinear associations. Methods: RF and OPGD on long-term high-resolution datasets. Results: CES showed initial increase then decline; dry-related extremes showed stronger associations than wet. Conclusions: empirical basis for region-specific adaptation under climate risk.

articles.title: An integrated land-use reclassification and scenario-simulation analysis of land system dynamics in China
articles.desc: Context: land-system change ecological consequences depend on use type/management, not cover alone. Objectives: integrated reclassification/scenario framework for China, dominant transition pathways 2000-2020/2030/2050. Methods: China Land Cover Dataset, remote sensing, 4 SSP-RCP scenarios. Results: cumulative transition 39.99% of territory; secondary vegetation central intermediate class. Conclusions: landscape planning should coordinate restoration, food security, habitat protection.

articles.title: Causal and threshold-dependent interactions of blue-green patterns in urban thermal regulation
articles.desc: Inconsistent findings regarding the impact of urban blue-green space patterns on regional thermal environments hinder the practical application of research in landscape ecology. This gap largely stems from a predominant focus on the global effects of landscape metrics, while their nonlinear inflection points, pairwise interactions, and underlying causal pathways have been insufficiently explored. This study aimed to (1) quantify the nonlinear and threshold effects of blue-green pattern metrics on land surface temperature (LST), (2) identify critical interactions between these pattern metrics, and (3) assess the direct and indirect pathways through which key drivers influence LST. The study was conducted in Suzhou, a humid subtropical canal city in China. We employed XGBoost-SHAP to decipher nonlinear effects and interactions, and further constructed a structural causal model (SCM) to quantify the direct and indirect pathways influencing LST. Blue-green pattern metrics effectively predicted seasonal land surface temperature (R 2 = 0.667–0.830). Water coverage (PLAND W ) was the dominant cooling factor across all seasons, followed by grassland coverage (PLAND G ) except in winter. Both water and forest coverage exhibited activation thresholds (2% for water; 5.32%–8.14% for forest) beyond which their cooling effects increased linearly. articles.title: Cumulative spatial assessment of observed wildlife-vehicle collisions based on indicator species thresholds
articles.desc: Context: traditional risk assessments assume linear relationship overlooking non-linear ecological thresholds. Objectives: quantify non-linear response thresholds of terrestrial vertebrates to landscape conditions, China. Methods: citizen science data, Threshold Indicator Taxa Analysis at 500m. Results: positive-response taxa show abrupt increases at thresholds; high-scoring segments concentrated in agricultural/urban SE China. Conclusions: hypothesis-generating framework for targeted mitigation

articles.title: Sociodemographic Factors and Land Use Shape Perceptions of Ecosystem Services in Reservoirs of Semiarid Regions
articles.desc: Community perceptions of ecosystem services shaped by local contexts/interactions with environment. Interviews with riverside communities, semiarid reservoirs, NE Brazil. 84% perceived services were provisioning, 12% cultural, 4% regulation/maintenance. Forested reservoirs showed higher regulation perception; human occupation areas showed higher provisioning perception. Highlights gap in ecological awareness among riparian communities; environmental education needed.

articles.title: Is Post-Fire Forest Recovery Fueled by Subsurface Nitrogen? Testing the N Bank Hypothesis
articles.desc: Nitrogen cycle paradox in northern conifer forests: wildfire depletes N stocks yet biomass/surface soils rapidly accumulate N post-fire. Testing N bank hypothesis across three stand ages of lodgepole pine recovering from fire, Wyoming USA. Mixed evidence of subsurface N mining/re-accumulation; nitrogenase activity estimates 3-5x higher than surface soil fixation. Suggests large soil N pools confer biogeochemical resilience to northern subalpine forests.

articles.title: Beneath the Surface: How the Declining Health of a Keystone Shrub Species Impacts Soil Carbon in a Temperate Mountain Ecosystem
articles.desc: Mountain pine key high-elevation species in European Alps, supports large SOC stocks; threatened by global change/invasive pathogens. Studied decline effects on SOC, Berchtesgaden National Park Germany, comparing forest/unstocked outcomes vs healthy/ailing stands. Transition to unstocked areas could cause 47.3% lower SOC; simulations show short-term gains shifting to long-term losses, 28.3 kilotons SOC loss. Demonstrates keystone species loss has long-lasting ecosystem consequences.

articles.title: Carbon Flux Dynamics in Rice-Wheat Systems Across Contrasting Climatic Regimes of Northern India Based on Eddy Covariance Measurements
articles.desc: Rice-wheat cropping system central to India's food security, grown under subtropical/temperate climates. NEE, Reco, GPP measured at Meerut (2008-2010) and Palampur (2017-2021) via eddy covariance. System acted as net carbon sink at both sites, higher sequestration at subtropical site; drought in 2009 reduced balance. PAR primary driver of GPP; supports sustainable agricultural management under climate change.

articles.title: Marsh Width and Elevation Govern Lateral Dynamics in Coastal Wetlands
articles.desc: Coastal wetland persistence controlled by vegetation/geomorphology/hydrodynamics interactions under sea level rise; lateral dynamics less studied than vertical accretion. Quantified salt marsh lateral erosion/migration over 80+ years, 75km Long Island south shore, 8 environmental drivers tested. Marshes migrating landward 0.44m/yr, eroding 0.20m/yr; wider/higher elevation marshes showed slower migration/erosion. Landscape configuration buffers coastlines from storm surges and forest dieback.

articles.title: Organic Matter Redox Status Predicts Methane Production in Boreal Peatland Ecosystems
articles.desc: Mechanisms controlling methane production in boreal peatlands not fully understood; redox-active organic matter (RAOM) reduction understudied mechanism suppressing methanogenesis. Compiled USA boreal peatland datasets, electron shuttling capacity assay, lab and field incubations. CH4 production linearly increased as RAOM reduced, explaining 20% (lab) and 60% (field) of production variance. RAOM redox state good predictor of CH4 production across boreal peatlands.

articles.title: Linking Scrub Mangroves Long-Term Foliar Net Primary Productivity and their Spatial Distribution in the Everglades: A Conceptual Model
articles.desc: Mangrove ecotype structural differences quantified but productivity/interaction knowledge gap remains, especially scrub mangrove wetlands. Evaluated decadal foliar NPP of scrub mangroves, lower Everglades Taylor Slough, 2012-2021, leaf-tagging. NPP 80% lower than riverine ecotypes at same latitude; explained by low phosphorus availability and long inundation duration. Proposes conceptual model for spatial configuration of scrub mangroves and freshwater flow reengineering impacts.

articles.title: Biodiversity, Fisheries, and Climate Benefits of Mangroves: A Nature-Based Solution for Ocean Ecosystems
articles.desc: Mangrove ecosystems globally recognized biodiversity hotspots, coastal resilience components, nursery habitats, carbon sequestration; declined due to urbanization/aquaculture/overexploitation. Review synthesizes biodiversity/fisheries functions and evaluates role as nature-based solution (NbS) for climate adaptation/mitigation. Integrates ecological/economic/governance/cultural perspectives across tropical/subtropical regions. Argues protecting/restoring mangroves critical for global biodiversit

articles.title: Isolating Effects of Temperature and Light on Nutrient Acquisition by Biofilm and Bryophyte Communities in Arctic Spring-Stream Ecosystems
articles.desc: Light/temperature seasonally coupled in most ecosystems making individual effects hard to isolate; Arctic spring-streams provide exception with constant temps/extreme light fluctuations. Measured nutrient demand/acquisition of biofilms/bryophytes, 5 Alaska spring-streams varying in temperature. Biofilm responses driven by temperature; bryophytes driven by light-temperature interaction. Demonstrates compartment-specific effects important for understanding ecosystem-level nutrient processes.

articles.title: Isoscapes of Particulate Organic Matter d13C and d15N Values in Chilean Coastal Waters
articles.desc: Stable isotope analysis widely used in marine ecology but depends on accounting for spatial/temporal baseline variability. First observation-based d13C/d15N isoscapes for POM, southeastern Pacific, ~2300km Chilean coastline, four cruises 2017-2018. Latitudinal gradient found; chlorophyll-a most consistent environmental predictor. Provides baseline for trophic ecology, animal movement, ecosystem connectivity studies in SE Pacific.

articles.title: Tidal Flats as Organic Matter Accumulation Zones: Depositional Patterns and Effects of Different Types of Detritus
articles.desc: Tidal flats recognized for climate change mitigation potential via carbon accumulation; organic matter predominantly allochthonous arriving in pulses. Characterized spatio-temporal wrack deposition patterns, compared marine vs terrestrial detritus effects on sediment OM. Terrestrial cordgrass wracks increased sediment OM/carbon storage potential; marine macroalgal wracks more labile, decomposed rapidly. Contributes to understanding tidal flat carbon cycling role under environmental change.

articles.title: Season-Specific Effects of Marine Heatwaves on Macrofaunal Community Composition and Ecosystem Processes
articles.desc: Marine heatwaves increasingly modify ecosystems, most prominent in summer; effects in other seasons less known. Four seasonal lab experiments on seasonal MHW effects on benthic community processes/structure, sediment cores. Strongest impact in summer, then autumn/spring/winter; summer showed migration into deeper sediment seeking thermal refuge. Demonstrates ecosystem process responses depend on seasonal context; improves prediction of vulnerability under climate extremes.

articles.title: The Too-Few Elephant Problem: Quantitative Analysis of Historical Elephant Tree-Toppling Rates Across Africa
articles.desc: Elephants were major driver of tree stem mortality in Africa; impacts now spatially constrained, most landscapes lack this ecological agent. Collated empirical treefall data with/without elephants, predicted past tree loss spatially. Elephants knock down 5.4% of trees per annum on average; mapping onto elephant-free areas reveals ~1/3 of woody biomass turnover norm lost. Urgent need for better theory on elephant-tree interactions informing restoration/degradation definitions.

articles.title: In Situ Evidence for Quantitative Nitrogen Fixation in a Temperate Perennial Grass Ecosystem
articles.desc: Non-symbiotic nitrogen fixation (NSNF) documented widely but magnitude/drivers uncertain due to methodological challenges. Measured NSNF via 15N2 tracer, field mesocosms with switchgrass, Michigan USA, early/mid growing season. Fixed N found throughout soil profile declining with depth; estimated NSNF inputs 2-12 kg N/ha/yr, 27-68% of annual plant N needs.

articles.title: Long-Term Reindeer Exclusion Leads to Higher Carbon Storage and Less Recalcitrant Carbon Compounds in Boreal Forest Soils
articles.desc: Reindeer reduce lichen biomass via consumption/trampling, cascading to microclimate/litter/soil carbon dynamics. Assessed 50+ year reindeer exclusion effects on plant biomass/soil carbon, 3 dry pine forest sites northern Finland. Lichen biomass 4.5x higher in exclosures; SOC stock 28% higher, more labile carbon pool composition. Long-term exclusion enhances SOC stocks, implications for carbon stability under grazing regime changes.

articles.title: Nitrogen and Phosphorus Availability Mediates the Effects of Bottom-Up Limitation on Orb-Weaver Spider Traits in an Amazonian Rainforest
articles.desc: Nutrient availability key driver of ecosystem functioning/food web structure; P and cation limitations may propagate to predators but poorly investigated in terrestrial systems. Used Amazon Fertilisation Experiment (AFEX), sampled two orb-weaving spider species measuring body size/fat reserves. Divergent species-specific responses to N/P addition reflecting foraging strategy differences. Indicates nutrient imbalances trigger species-specific life-history trait responses with food web implication

articles.title: Diverse Impacts of Urbanization on Vegetation Growth and Its Driving Factors in Ten Global Megacities
articles.desc: Urbanization effects on vegetation growth within megacities underexplored regarding intensity gradients/temporal instability. Compared urban expansion/EVI trends/driving factors across 10 global megacities 2000-2018. All cities expanded; EVI increased significantly only in Paris/Tokyo, most showed heterogeneous greening/browning at pixel scale. Vegetation greening context-dependent balance among removal, management, water/heat limitation, socioeconomic capacity.

articles.title: Global patterns in plant-pollinator specialization
articles.desc: Pollination is a key ecological process sustaining biodiversity and food security, yet global patterns of plant–pollinator specialization remain unresolved. Using a global dataset of quantitative plant–pollinator networks (>3,400 networks, >110,000 interactions), we show that specialization is latitudinally structured, but not as a single directional pattern. We find no consistent monotonic increase or decrease in specialization towards the Equator. Instead, network-level and pollinator specialization peak at low northern latitudes near the tropical–subtropical boundary, whereas plant specialization is hemispherically asymmetric. Climate is most often the best-supported predictor of specialization compared with latitude, biodiversity and environmental productivity. Network-level specialization declines with increasing mean annual temperature, with strong group-specific differences. Precipitation exerts nonlinear effects: plant specialization peaks at intermediate precipitation but is lower at the wettest sites, whereas pollinator specialization is lower at intermediate precipitation, although often in interaction with temperature. Pollinator groups diverge strongly, especially in contrasting precipitation-related patterns between birds and insects. These findings show that global plant–pollinator specialization is structured by latitude and climate in complex and taxon-specific ways, with implications for uneven responses of pollination networks to future climatic change.
